title: How to Teach Math With Debate and AI While Learning About All Three
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Stefan Bauschard describes a 28-page classroom packet he built with Claude and proofed with ChatGPT to teach exponential models in Algebra II by combining debate, AI, and a real dataset - Netflix's own disclosed subscriber counts from 2016 through 2020. Students fit an exponential model that matches the historical data almost perfectly, then discover the model's extrapolation to 2025 overshot Netflix's actual disclosed membership by roughly 76%, making the central lesson that a good statistical fit does not by itself license a forecast. The packet layers debate on top of the math (targeting only genuinely contestable claims, never settled numerical answers) and AI on top of both, with students using AI to identify and verify evidence rather than simply generate arguments, and an explicit academic-honesty protocol that has students mark every sentence as authored, machine-written, or machine-drafted-and-rewritten without penalty, so they have no incentive to conceal AI use. Bauschard is careful to frame the packet as an untested proof of concept - never run with actual students - and asks working math teachers to stress-test its timing, prerequisites, and difficulty curve before adoption, while arguing the underlying structure transfers to other subjects.
points: The lesson uses a real dataset - Netflix's disclosed subscriber counts from 2016-2020 - to build a near-perfect exponential growth model, then reveals the model's 2025 forecast overshot actual results by roughly 76%, making the fit-versus-forecast gap the lesson's central point.
Bauschard's design rule for classroom debate is that it only works on genuinely contestable questions, never on settled math questions with a single correct answer.

The AI-disclosure protocol requires every sentence in a student's debate case to be marked authored, machine-written, or machine-drafted-and-rewritten, with no point penalty for any mark, explicitly to prevent students from concealing AI use.
The author explicitly frames the 28-page packet as an unvalidated proof of concept requiring a working math teacher's review of timing, prerequisites, and difficulty before classroom use.
quotes: Those five points fit an exponential model almost perfectly. The base works out to about 1.23, roughly 23% annual growth, and the model matches every given point to within 3.4%.
That gap is the lesson. Fit and forecast are separate claims, and being good at the first does not by itself license the second.
Debate in a math class fails when teachers stage arguments over questions that have answers. Build a debate around a settled question and you have built a quiz with more noise in it.

Most AI-in-the-classroom debate activities fail identically. The student asks a model for arguments, the model supplies them, and the reasoning the debate existed to produce never happens. The AI absorbs the authorship.

Students disclose rather than abstain. Each sentence in a case gets marked as authored, machine-written, or machine-drafted and rewritten. No mark costs points, because the moment a mark costs points students stop marking honestly and you have taught concealment instead.
A ban teaches students that the issue is whether they get caught. Disclosure puts the real issue in front of them: whether they can answer for what the machine gave them.
It is a proof of concept. It has never been run with students.
